title: charsets: Optimize getting UTF-8 strings with an accumulator
description:
Add all the valid bytes at once when we get to the end of the
length (or hit an invalid sequence) instead of one byte or character
at a time. This makes for a considerable speedup.

notes.body:
Failing on Windows:

```
...\epan\charsets.c(388,19): error C2220: the following warning is treated as an error
...\epan\charsets.c(388,19): error C2220:         length -= valid_bytes;
...\epan\charsets.c(388,19): error C2220:                   ^
...\epan\charsets.c(388,19): warning C4267: '-=': conversion from 'size_t' to 'gint', possible loss of data
...\epan\charsets.c(388,19): warning C4267:         length -= valid_bytes;
...\epan\charsets.c(388,19): warning C4267:                   ^
```
What's the reason for the huge `#if 0` block?

This is still somewhat a draft, I will mark it as such.

On Linux, both gcc and clang, very long strings that are mostly in the ASCII range are two to three times faster with that code enabled, but I want to  get a better idea of what the performance impact is on strings with lots of two to four byte characters is.

My testing (and godbolt) verified that gcc and clang are also smart enough to optimize our pntoh32 and phtoh64 into single fetch 32/64 bit and byte reverse instructions, but msvc doesn't seem to be quite as efficient.

I will remove those lines before actually committing this (after cleaning up whatever MSVC doesn't like), and maybe keep testing them on another branch.

Doing the memcpy all at once is an unconditional performance improvement, so that it's worth pushing alone first.
We should move the code to wsutil too and replace the GLib functions everywhere.

> My testing (and godbolt) verified that gcc and clang are also smart enough to optimize our pntoh32 and phtoh64 into single fetch 32/64 bit and byte reverse instructions, but msvc doesn't seem to be quite as efficient.

Not too long ago, I saw a blog post in which somebody argued that using various tricks to optimize unaligned fetches of data in a particular byte order was no longer necessary, and that we should just Trust The Compiler.  I've no idea with which compilers they tested, so maybe that's premature (or maybe they're in camp Who Cares About Windows or camp Who Cares About MSVC).

Using [Mike Godbolt's Compiler Explorer](https://godbolt.org):

GCC for x86-64, with -Os, seems to optimize 4-byte and 8-byte unaligned big-endian and little-endian loading since GCC 5.1, but doesn't optimize 2-byte unaligned big-endian and little-endian loading until GCC 10.1.

GCC for ARM64, with -Os, does it for all of them starting with GCC 5.4, although it doesn't use rev16 (16-bit byte-swap, I assume) until 10.2 (was it added to A64 later?).  For ARM32, it's not so easy, presumably because unaligned loads aren't guaranteed to work, but it does a variety of different things in different versions.

Clang for x86-64, with -Os, does it for all of them starting with Clang 5.0.

Clang for ARM64, with -Os, does it for all of them starting with Clang 9.0.  For ARM32, it's not so easy, presumably because unaligned loads aren't guaranteed to work.

GCC for z/Architecture ("s390x") does it for all of them with the oldest GCC they have, 11.2.0.  (I'm not sure how LLGF differs from good old-fashioned L, given that support for unaligned accesses has been a standard feature since System/370, but I digress....)  There seems to be fairly optimal code for newer versions of GCC for big-endian and little-endian PPC64/Power ISA 64 as well.  GCC 12 even does its best for MIPS, where unaligned host-endian 32-bit and 64-bit loads can be built from "load left" and "load right" instructions, but byte-swapping is a lot of work.

And MSVC hasn't picked up the "special hacks for networking stacks and packet sniffers" stuff yet, whether for x86-64, x86, or ARM64, even with /Os or /Ot.  icc (Intel's compiler) hasn't picked them up, either.

So, the `pnto*` functions in `wsutil/pint.h` _should_ (for now) be optimized for MSVC and icc on x86 (although we're dropping 32 bit support on Windows) because they are called often and those compilers don't realize what we're doing, whereas on gcc and clang they are optimized well. (And presumably for esoteric architectures with CHAR_BIT != 8 they should be left as written for the compiler in any case.) However, I'll leave that to a different MR.

For ASCII, and ASCII compatible encodings (including UTF-8), bytes with the sign bit 0 are copied unconditionally, which means that it can be significantly faster (2-4x) on some architectures to load 32 or 64 bit values, examine all the sign bits, and skip 4 or 8 bytes at a time if all 0, otherwise behave as currently byte by byte, at least for input that is mostly ASCII (which includes most Western European languages). For input that is a fair amount of ASCII, and with the right CPU support (LZCNT/CLZ/cntlzd on x86/ARM/PPC, `_mm[256|512]_movepi8_mask` in AVX512 for x86) it *might* even be faster when the sign bits are not all zero to then search for the first sign bit set (avoiding the BSR/LZCNT question of what to do at zero) in order to skip 1-7 ASCII bytes. For input that is mostly non ASCII, it's probably slower, though it's a question of how much slower (and it might not be that bad, considering that non ASCII input is already in the slow path).

For ASCII encoding itself, it's probably correct to optimize for the case where the input is mostly ASCII. Other encodings would take more testing. All that is another MR, so for now I'm going to commit this part, which is unambiguously faster on all input.

Moving the UTF-8 function (what about other encodings?) to `wsutil/` and using it more broadly makes sense, but I think I'll leave that to another MR. Similarly, some of these functions should probably take a `size_t` as input, and most of them should return the length of the converted string, since we try to handle internal NUL, as well as some status about whether conversion failed.

An addendum:

While MSVC and icc do not optimize the shifts and masks strategy, both *do* optimize approaches using memcpy.

```
    uint64_t tmp;
    memcpy(&tmp, p, sizeof(tmp));
    return __builtin_bswap64(tmp); // on icc, clang, gcc:  _byteswap_uint64 on MSVC
```

And in fact replace these with single `MOV` and `bswap` instructions, as expected (and `ldr` and `rev` on ARM64 for MSVC).

So one possible approach is to, at least for 16, 32, and 64 bit, simply switch to the memcpy implementation.
